newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Unocal plays Afghan waiting game on pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Unocal plays Afghan waiting game on pipeline.

text.p: There may be little end in sight to fighting in Afghanistan, but U.S. oil major Unocal Corp, planning to build a $2-billion natural gas pipeline across the war-ravaged country, is for now prepared to wait it out.
"It's a waiting game," John Imle, Unocal's president, told Reuters in an interview in Ashgabat late Wednesday. "We've been disappointed that Afghanistan remains a country of turmoil."
But Imle said Unocal was for the moment prepared to sit and wait. "There are a lot of gas and oil reserves to back both these pipeline systems. It'll be a good deal on a stand-alone basis," he said.

Unocal, with Saudi Arabia's Delta Oil, aims to build the 1,500 km (1,000 mile) gas pipeline from the Turkmen-Afghan border to Multan in northern Pakistan. There is also an option to extend the pipeline to northern India.
The gas would come from the huge Dauletabad gas field in southeast Turkmenistan, and over half the route would be located on Afghan territory.
Imle said Dauletabad had 30 years supply to pipe 20 billion cubic metres (bcm) a year to south Asian markets.

Uzbek President Islam Karimov, speaking at a regional summit in Turkmenistan on Wednesday, said the Afghan war threatened continued isolation from world markets for the clutch of ex-Soviet Central Asian states desperate for cash to bolster their embattled economies.
"If the war continues in Afghanistan, not one project here means anything," Karimov said.

Observers who once scoffed at the idea of building a pipeline through Afghanistan, a prey to a myriad armed factions, are taking the project more seriously now that the purist Islamic Talban militia have placed three quarters of the country under its control.
Crucial to the project, say observers, is a recognised government which Unocal and other energy firms can deal with.
A western diplomat in the Turkmen capital Ashgabat said: "Oil majors don't put up that kind of money for nothing."
The pipeline project was born of what Imle said is landlocked Central Asia's transport bottleneck, with the clutch of ex-Soviet states reliant on existing Soviet-era pipelines controlled by Russia.
"Transportation is the issue," said Imle. "There is plenty of oil and gas but we decided to enter Central Asia with a transport project," he said.
An oil pipeline is also planned to follow the gas pipeline route, with export capacity to the Arabian Sea pencilled in at one million barrels a day.
Imle said Unocal would aim the pipeline at Kazakhstan, with vast oil reserves in the west of the former Soviet republic, and even Russian producers in western Siberia.
"Sweet crude landing on the Indian Ocean is a dollar or two higher than Urals blend landing in the Black Sea," Imle said.
He said Unocal was already active in finding and establishing a market for the gas in Pakistan, particularly in power generation.
As well as ongoing political uncertainty in Afghanistan, Unocal faces a battle with another company for rights to the pipeline project -- Argentinian independent Bridas Energy Corp.
Bridas is suing Unocal for what it called "tortuous interference" in a plan Bridas developed to export Turkmen gas to Pakistan via Afghanistan. U.S. court hearings are pencilled in for November.
"We feel that there's no foundation for the lawsuit," Imle said. "We expect to defend ourselves very vigorously when it comes to trial."

It is also unclear how a memorandum signed on Wednesday between the Presidents of Turkmenistan, Iran and Turkey to transport gas from the Dauletabad field to Turkey via Iran would affect the Unocal plan.
Unocal officials were not immediately available for comment.
